When Ka'b and Ibn Abi Hadrad raised their voices over a debt in the mosque, the Prophet had Ka'b remit half and told the debtor to pay the rest.
An Israelite debtor who found no boat sent a thousand dinars to his creditor in a log thrown into the sea, and the creditor found it on sawing the wood.
The Prophet asked Allah's mercy for one lenient in buying, selling and claiming his money; Allah forgave men who gave debtors time and forgave those in hardship.
A rich man delaying repayment is unjust, and a debt transferred to a rich debtor should be accepted; the Prophet prays over a debtor once Abu Qatada takes it on.
The Prophet will not lead a debtor's funeral prayer until Abu Qatada undertakes to pay the debt.
The Prophet prayed over dead debtors only if they left enough to repay; once wealthy through conquests, he took on believers' debts, their wealth going to their heirs.
A creditor, rude in one report, is given an older camel than he was owed, and the Prophet says the best people repay others' rights generously.
The Prophet pays for Jabir's camel later and mortgages armour for food on credit; Allah repays for a borrower meaning to repay, and he would keep gold only for debts.
The Prophet repays a harsh creditor with an older camel, as the best repay handsomely; a merchant who eased his debtors was forgiven, and Jabir is repaid with extra.
The Prophet blesses Jabir's palms so his father's debts are paid with dates to spare; he seeks refuge from debt and takes on dead believers' debts, heirs getting their property.
Delay by a rich debtor is injustice, a creditor has the right to speak, and one finding his own goods with a bankrupt has most right to them.
An Israelite lends money for a fixed period; the Prophet measures out Jabir's dates to his dead father's creditors without lessening them, and buys Jabir's tired camel.
Hearing Ka'b and Ibn Abi Hadrad argue loudly over a debt in the mosque, the Prophet has Ka'b drop half and tells the debtor to repay the rest.
Ka'b, arguing loudly with his debtor, is told by the Prophet's gesture to drop half the debt, and he takes half.
When creditors harshly demanded the debt of Jabir's father, martyred at Uhud, the Prophet blessed his date-palms, and their fruit paid them in full with much left over.
The Prophet paid Jabir what he owed him and more, weighing out the price of the camel Jabir had sold him with an extra amount.
When a creditor demanded his debt harshly, the Prophet stopped his companions, saying he had the right to speak, and repaid him an older camel, as the best repay best.
Owing a camel of a certain age, the Prophet let its owner demand it and repaid him an older camel, saying the best repay their debts most handsomely.
The Prophet settled loud debt disputes: one who swore not to ease his debtor gave way, and Ka'b remitted half of what Ibn Abu Hadrad owed him.
The Prophet blessed the dates of Jabir's indebted father so all creditors were paid with thirteen wasqs left, and had Ka'b remit half of Ibn Abu Hadrad's debt.
The Prophet mentioned a man who asked an Israelite to lend him a thousand dinars, and was lent them for a fixed period.
Jabir's father, martyred at Uhud, left heavy debts; the Prophet sat on the biggest date heap and measured out until all were paid, the heaps still seeming whole.
At Al-Jamal Az-Zubair asks his son to pay his debts, seeking Allah's help; Abdullah sells property, settles 2.2 million, calls claimants for four Hajj seasons, then divides the estate.
The Prophet left the funeral prayer of debtors who left nothing to others, but after Allah gave him victories he paid believers' debts himself, their wealth going to heirs.
